retrieved_evidence.title: TCP SYN Flood and Handshake Exhaustion
retrieved_evidence.text: A TCP SYN flood is a classic denial-of-service attack exploiting the TCP three-way handshake. The attacker sends a rapid stream of TCP packets with the SYN flag set, initiating connections without sending the completing ACK packet. This leaves half-open connection entries in the target system's backlog queue, eventually exhausting connection table memory and denying access to legitimate clients. Primary network telemetry indicators include a surging syn_count, disproportionate syn_flag_number, and drastically reduced ACK completion ratios.
retrieved_evidence.source_citation: CERT Advisory CA-1996-21 / RFC 793: Transmission Control Protocol Specification (1981)

retrieved_evidence.title: Normal IoT Baseline Telemetry and Rate Patterns
retrieved_evidence.text: In benign IoT network environments, connected sensor telemetry exhibits periodic heartbeat signals, deterministic polling intervals, and bounded transmission rates. Occasional burst traffic and rate increases occur legitimately during firmware updates, scheduled cloud state synchronization, or temporary network reconnects. Benign telemetry flows generally maintain consistent TCP flag ratios and stable interarrival times, whereas attack bursts exhibit severe rate anomalies coupled with abnormal flag distributions.
retrieved_evidence.source_citation: NIST SP 800-213: IoT Device Cybersecurity Guidance for the Federal Government (2021)

retrieved_evidence.title: Network Reconnaissance, Port Scanning, and Host Probing
retrieved_evidence.text: Reconnaissance attacks gather intelligence regarding active IP addresses, open ports, and operating system versions before launching exploits. Techniques include TCP SYN stealth scans, full connect scans, UDP port probing, and ICMP ping sweeps. In flow telemetry, reconnaissance produces a large number of very short-lived connections (low flow_duration), elevated syn_count or rst_count, high ratio of RST packets returned by closed ports, and minimal payload size (low Tot sum and AVG).
retrieved_evidence.source_citation: NIST SP 800-94: Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS) (2012)

retrieved_evidence.title: MQTT Protocol Security and IoT Publish/Connect Floods
retrieved_evidence.text: MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is an asynchronous publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained IoT sensors, running over TCP port 1883 or TLS port 8883. Common IoT DoS attacks targeting MQTT brokers include Connect Floods and Publish Floods, where attackers rapidly open client sessions or broadcast excessive high-frequency payloads across popular topics. These attacks cause memory exhaustion and queue starvation on the central broker, manifesting as surges in TCP flow rates and payload counts.

retrieved_evidence.title: Limitations of Anomaly-Based Network Intrusion Detection
retrieved_evidence.text: Machine learning and statistical anomaly detection models identify statistical deviations from a modeled benign traffic baseline. However, an anomaly score does not equal an attack classification. Unsupervised models (such as autoencoders and Mahalanobis scorers) frequently trigger false alarms due to non-malicious shifts in network behavior, including backup syncs, microservice initialization, or changes in protocol mix. Scientific validation requires that model attributions be treated as hypotheses requiring corroboration from endpoint telemetry, packet headers, or independent logs before confirming malicious activity.
retrieved_evidence.source_citation: Sommer & Paxson: Outside the Closed World: On Using Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection (IEEE S&P 2010)
retrieved_evidence.provenance: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P 2010)

retrieved_evidence.title: UDP Flood and Reflection Amplification Attacks
retrieved_evidence.text: UDP is a connectionless, stateless transport protocol that does not use a handshake. In a UDP flood attack, adversaries send massive volumes of high-rate UDP datagrams to random ports on the target. Because UDP does not verify sender addresses, attackers routinely spoof source IPs to reflect amplified responses from public resolvers onto victim networks. In network telemetry, UDP floods present as extreme spikes in UDP packet counts, massive aggregate byte volume (Tot sum), elevated transmission Rate, and collapsed packet interarrival times (IAT).
retrieved_evidence.source_citation: CISA Alert TA14-017A: UDP-Based Amplification Attacks / RFC 768 (1980)
retrieved_evidence.provenance: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Alert TA14-017A
